"Breathe with me," Teo said. "In for four. Out for four."

"Sorry," he said.

"Gran?" Clara's voice came thin and sleepy. "Is something wrong?"

"Nothing's wrong," Marta said. "I only wanted to see if it worked."

"It works."

"Good." Marta looked at the ceiling, at the sugar bowl, at Biscuit watching from the windowsill. "Then tell me about your day. All of it. I've got time."

"Then you drive him on Thursdays," Ruth said.

"From Toledo?" Danny said.

Ruth's daughter, Maya, sixteen and three weeks into her learner's permit, watched from the doorway.

"I do not," said Ruth, who did.

"You could sit in the passenger seat," Maya told Walter. "Tuesdays and Thursdays. You tell me where to turn."

Walter looked at the keys, then at his granddaughter. He split the clementine and slid half across the table to her.

"You'll take Delancey slow," he said.

"Slow," Maya agreed.

Ruth pocketed the keys before anyone could change their mind. Danny crossed the kitchen and squeezed his father's shoulder, and Walter let him.

Rosa Achterberg spent March measuring trail grades on a topographic map with a protractor, and by June she had a number: the east route up Mount Kessel never got steeper than fourteen percent, except for one stretch the guidebook called the Staircase.

"We'll carry you up the Staircase," Benji Okafor said at the trailhead, cinching his pack.

"You'll carry the chair," Rosa said. "I'll carry me."

"Again," Rosa said.

Above the treeline the wind got loud, and the path flattened into a ridge of crushed stone. Rosa rolled the last two hundred yards with nobody touching the chair. Ilse walked beside her, the slack strap coiled over her arm.

At the cairn, Rosa set her brakes, peeled off her gloves, and studied the blisters the leather had failed to prevent.

"Next year," she said, "the west route."

Benji lay flat on the rock and groaned.

Mara smiled and lifted her bow. Out in the corridor, Tobias pressed his ear to the door and began, very softly, to count her measures.

She was a brindle mutt with one folded ear, and for two days she walked the wrong way along the ring road, drinking from gutters. On the third morning the wind turned and carried a thin thread of burnt sugar. That was the Marek bakery, four streets from home. Biscuit put her nose into it and followed.

The river stopped her. She paced the embankment until Tomasz, a tram driver eating his lunch on the steps, tossed her a crust and watched her limp onto the footbridge behind a line of schoolchildren. A girl named Odile held out a hand. Biscuit sniffed it, licked the salt off, and kept walking.

Past the bridge came the rail yards, where a yellow dog bit her shoulder over a chicken bone. Biscuit let him have it. She crawled under the fence and slept beneath a parked lorry until the cold woke her and the sugar smell rose again, stronger now, because Mrs. Marek lit her ovens at four.

Grey light was coming when she turned onto Linden Street. Every lamppost carried a paper with her face on it, and the ink had run in the rain.

Jonah, nine years old, sat on the front step in his coat, where he had sat every morning that week. He looked up from his cereal bowl. The spoon hit the pavement.

Biscuit did not run. She walked the last ten metres, leaned her whole weight against his knees, and slept.
